stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. Write both budget constraints and draw their frontiers in the same figure, with $C_1$ and $C_2$ in thousands of rupees on the horizontal and vertical axes.
solution: For income $(a,b)$ in thousands, saving $a-C_1\geq0$ yields $C_2=b+a-C_1$, while borrowing $C_1-a\geq0$ requires repayment $3(C_1-a)$, yielding $C_2=b-3(C_1-a)$. Feasible consumption lies on or below the piecewise frontier in the nonnegative quadrant. Plot A through $(0,40),(25,15),(30,0)$ and B through $(0,45),(15,30),(25,0)$. Their frontiers intersect at $(17.5,22.5)$.
hint: Separate the saving and borrowing segments.

stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. B borrows Rs. 5,000 in period 1. Give an example of a consumption profile which, if chosen by A, proves their preferences differ, with explanation.
answer: For example A choosing $(C_1,C_2)=(15,25)$ thousand rupees.
solution: B chooses $(20,15)$. A can afford $(20,20)$, which strictly dominates B's choice, so A's chosen bundle must be strictly preferred to $(20,15)$. But $(15,25)$ is strictly inside B's budget (at $C_1=15$ B can consume $C_2=30$). Thus if A chose $(15,25)$ and both had the same monotonic preferences, B would have available a strictly preferable bundle to his chosen one, a contradiction. The same revealed-preference argument applies to any A frontier choice with $C_1\leq17.5$.
hint: Test each chosen bundle against the other budget.

stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. Now A and B have the same preferences and B borrows Rs. 5,000. (i) [6 marks] If A lends in period 1, find the maximum lending consistent with common preferences. (ii) [6 marks] Is B better off than A?
answer: (i) Lending must be strictly below Rs. 7,500 (supremum Rs. 7,500). (ii) A is strictly better off than B.
solution: B chooses $b=(20,15)$ in thousands. A can afford $(20,20)$, so monotonicity implies her chosen bundle $a$ is strictly preferred to $b$. If A lends, her choice is $(x,40-x)$ with $x\leq25$. Such a bundle is feasible for B whenever $x\leq17.5$: below 15 it lies below B's saving frontier, and from 15 onward $40-x\leq75-3x$ exactly when $x\leq17.5$. Common preferences therefore require $x>17.5$, otherwise B could choose a bundle strictly preferred to $b$. Thus saving $25-x<7.5$ thousand. The common frontier point at 17.5 is also ruled out, so the bound is strict; the source's word maximum should be read as supremum. The earlier comparison already proves A strictly better off.
hint: Locate the intersection of the budgets and apply strict monotonicity.
notes: No attained maximum under the stated monotonicity: Rs. 7,500 is a strict upper bound/supremum, not an admissible maximum.

stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. Describe all Pareto-efficient allocations.
answer: In agent 1 coordinates: $Y_1=2X_1$, $0\leq X_1\leq1/2$, or $Y_1=1$, $1/2\leq X_1\leq1$.
solution: Fix agent 2's utility, equivalently the resource cost $t=2X_1+Y_1\in[0,3]$. Efficiency maximizes $X_1Y_1$ subject to this cost and $0\leq X_1,Y_1\leq1$. The unconstrained maximizer has $Y_1=2X_1$, hence $X_1=t/4,Y_1=t/2$ for $t\leq2$. For $t\geq2$, the upper bound $Y_1=1$ binds and $X_1=(t-1)/2$. These maximizers, including both endpoints, trace the stated frontier. Any other allocation permits higher utility for agent 1 at unchanged utility for agent 2.
hint: Maximize the product at a fixed cost $2X_1+Y_1$.

stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. An allocation is envy-free if $u_1(X_1,Y_1)\geq u_1(X_2,Y_2)$ and $u_2(X_2,Y_2)\geq u_2(X_1,Y_1)$. (i) [6 marks] Are all efficient allocations envy-free, and are all envy-free allocations efficient? Prove or give counterexamples. (ii) [6 marks] Describe all envy-free allocations.
answer: Both implications are false. Envy-free set: $0\leq x,y\leq1$, $x+y\geq1$, $2x+y\leq3/2$, where $(x,y)=(X_1,Y_1)$.
solution: (i) Giving everything to agent 1 is efficient but agent 2 envies her. Equal division $(1/2,1/2)$ is envy-free but inefficient: for small $\epsilon>0$, replace agent 1's bundle by $(1/2-\epsilon,1/2+2\epsilon)$. Agent 2's utility stays fixed while agent 1's product rises by $\epsilon/2-2\epsilon^2>0$. (ii) Agent 1's no-envy inequality is $xy\geq(1-x)(1-y)$, equivalent to $x+y\geq1$. Agent 2's is $2(1-x)+(1-y)\geq2x+y$, equivalent to $2x+y\leq3/2$. Intersect these with the unit square; the triangle has vertices $(0,1),(1/4,1),(1/2,1/2)$.
hint: Write both no-envy inequalities using the resource constraints.
notes: Part (ii) is on user PDF page 17.

stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. Each agent is endowed with half a unit of each good. Prove without direct computation that a competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient and envy-free.
answer: Equal incomes imply no envy; local nonsatiation and competitive optimization imply Pareto efficiency.
solution: At common prices both agents have the same wealth, since their endowments coincide. Each can therefore afford the other's equilibrium bundle. Individual optimality implies neither strictly prefers the other's bundle, establishing envy-freeness. For efficiency, suppose a feasible allocation made everyone weakly better off and someone strictly better off. Optimality and local nonsatiation require each weakly better bundle to cost at least that agent's wealth, and any strictly better bundle to cost strictly more. Summing would exceed the value of total endowments, contradicting feasibility and market clearing. This is the first welfare theorem.
hint: Combine identical budget sets with the first welfare theorem.

stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. How much music does each play independently? Find efficient music levels and compare, with economic intuition.
solution: Each ignores the effect on the other and sets $8-4m_i=0$, giving 2. With transfers, efficiency maximizes total utility, whose music component is $8(m_1+m_2)-(7/2)(m_1^2+m_2^2)$. FOCs $8-7m_i=0$ give $8/7$. Independent play is excessive because its negative external effect is ignored.
hint: Compare private and social marginal benefits.

stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. Individual 2 considers giving a headphone to individual 1 and gets no utility from gift-giving itself. What is the maximum price she would pay?
solution: Without headphones, individual 1 plays $m_1=2$, causing individual 2 loss $(3/2)2^2=6$. A headphone removes this external harm while leaving her own optimal music unchanged. Quasilinearity makes the avoided utility loss her maximum monetary willingness to pay.
hint: Value the external harm removed by the gift.

stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. A headphone costs Rs. 11. Should the flatmates jointly buy it, split the cost equally and commit to listening only via the headphone?
answer: Yes; each gains Rs. 0.50 in utility-equivalent terms.
solution: Each initially receives own-music benefit $8(2)-2(2)^2=8$ minus harm 6, giving 2 before money holdings. Headphones preserve own benefit 8, remove harm 6 and cost each $11/2=5.5$, giving 2.5. Hence each gains 0.5, so the arrangement is mutually beneficial.
hint: Compare each person’s avoided harm with half the price.
notes: Question continues onto user PDF page 18.

stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. Now individual 1 owns the player and can prohibit individual 2 from playing. She offers a take-it-or-leave-it contract: she plays $\bar m_1$, individual 2 may play $\bar m_2$ for payment $T$. If rejected, individual 1 chooses her music unilaterally and individual 2 plays none. Find optimal $\bar m_1,\bar m_2,T$ and explain.
solution: Upon rejection, individual 1 chooses 2 and individual 2's utility excluding money is $-6$. Acceptance requires $8m_2-2m_2^2-(3/2)m_1^2-T\geq-6$. Individual 1 sets the largest acceptable transfer $T=8m_2-2m_2^2-(3/2)m_1^2+6$. Her resulting utility is total music surplus plus 6, so she chooses the efficient levels $m_1=m_2=8/7$. Substitution gives $T=64/7-32/7+6=74/7$. She captures the gains over individual 2's outside option. This assumes acceptance at indifference and no binding transfer/wealth constraint.
hint: Use the other flatmate’s participation constraint to eliminate the transfer.

stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. Write profit as a function of both employment quantities.
solution: Revenue is output price times production. Subtract the wage bill for each province to obtain the stated expression.
hint: Subtract both wage bills from revenue.

stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. The employer maximizes $u(\pi(N^A,N^B),N^A,N^B)$, with $u_\pi>0$, direct $u_A>0$ and direct $u_B<0$. Write the first-order conditions assuming an interior solution.
solution: By the chain rule, differentiate utility with respect to each employment quantity, including both its profit effect and its direct taste effect. Evaluate $F\prime$ at $N^A+N^B$ and all utility partials at the chosen allocation. These are necessary interior FOCs; the stated monotonicity conditions alone do not guarantee sufficiency.
hint: Include the direct preference effect as well as the profit effect.

stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. The employer maximizes $u(\pi(N^A,N^B),N^A,N^B)$, with $u_\pi>0$, direct $u_A>0$ and direct $u_B<0$. Do employees from both provinces receive the same wage in equilibrium? If not, who receives more and by how much?
answer: With both types employed at an interior optimum, $W^A-W^B=(u_A-u_B)/u_\pi>0$.
solution: Rearranging the FOCs gives $W^A=PF\prime+u_A/u_\pi$ and $W^B=PF\prime+u_B/u_\pi$. Thus preferred A workers receive more despite identical marginal productivity; the wage gap is the difference in direct utility effects divided by marginal utility of profit. The claim is conditional on both labour types being hired at an interior optimum; corner hiring or market supply conditions not supplied cannot be characterized from these FOCs alone.
hint: Subtract the two interior conditions.

stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Derive the slope of an indifference curve in the earnings–consumption plane.
solution: Along an indifference curve, $0=du=u_c\,dc+(u_l/w)\,dy$. Rearranging gives the slope. Its positivity reflects that more labour earnings require additional consumption to compensate for the disutility of working.
hint: Totally differentiate utility while holding its level fixed.

stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Show the utility-maximizing earnings and consumption in a figure with the budget line and indifference curves.
answer: Budget $c=y/p$, $0\leq y\leq w\bar L$; an interior optimum satisfies $-u_l/(wu_c)=1/p$.
solution: Draw the budget segment from $(0,0)$ to $(w\bar L,w\bar L/p)$ with slope $1/p$. Indifference curves slope upward; higher utility lies above a given curve at fixed earnings. The highest attainable curve is tangent to the segment at an interior solution, equating its slope with $1/p$. Equivalently $-u_l/u_c=w/p$. A corner at the time bound or zero work must be checked when the tangency is not feasible; positive consumption is not otherwise guaranteed by the stated general utility.
hint: The feasible segment has a positive slope in these axes.

stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Experiment 1: increase $w$. In the same figure show which budget or indifference curves change and compare the old and new earnings and consumption, with explanation.
answer: The budget ray’s slope stays $1/p$ and its endpoint extends. Preferences in the earnings–consumption coordinates change; welfare weakly rises, but earnings/hours need not move unambiguously under the stated general assumptions.
solution: At the same $(y,c)$, a larger wage requires less labour $l=y/w$, so utility rises. The budget segment remains on $c=y/p$, extending to $y=w_{new}\bar L$. Draw the new indifference map using $u(c,y/w_{new})$, with the new optimum where its relevant curve touches the budget. The old labour–consumption choice can be replicated with less labour or can finance more consumption, so welfare weakly improves. In labour–leisure coordinates the wage increase has opposing substitution and income effects on labour. Neither normality nor restrictions on the cross partial are stated, so a universal movement of earnings or consumption should not be asserted; along the budget earnings and consumption move together. Under customary additional normality assumptions their standard directions can be shown in the diagram.
hint: Changing wage changes the preference map when the horizontal axis is earnings.
notes: General concavity and monotonicity do not state normality; diagram must not impose an unconditional earnings/labour response.

stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Experiment 2: instead impose a proportional income tax $\tau$, so disposable income is $(1-\tau)y$. Draw old and new optima and show the budget and preference changes, comparing outcomes.
answer: For $0<\tau<1$, budget rotates down to $c=(1-\tau)y/p$; the preference map is unchanged and welfare weakly falls. Labour/earnings response is generally ambiguous.
solution: In the same earnings–consumption axes, retain the original indifference curves because $w$ is unchanged. Rotate the budget segment clockwise through the origin from slope $1/p$ to $(1-\tau)/p$, keeping horizontal endpoint $w\bar L$. An interior new optimum satisfies $-u_l/(wu_c)=(1-\tau)/p$. The feasible consumption set contracts, so utility cannot rise. The lower net wage produces opposing substitution and income effects on labour; without further preference restrictions its sign, and thus gross earnings, is ambiguous. Consumption also has no universal sign under the fully general preferences stated.
hint: The tax changes net purchasing power, not the labour required for gross earnings.
notes: Question continues onto user PDF page 21. Proportional tax assumed between zero and one.

stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Write separate period-2 and period-3 budget constraints.
solution: Period-2 resources are labour earnings minus repayment of the education loan. They finance consumption and saving. In period 3, gross saving returns are the sole resources and are consumed.
hint: Account for education debt before allocating period-2 resources.

stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Set up the utility maximization problem, identifying the choices.
solution: The choices are education $e$ and saving $s$; equivalently choose all four variables $e,s,c_2,c_3$ under the two budgets and positive consumption. Feasibility requires $0<s<wh(e)-(1+r)e$. Substitute the budgets to obtain the answer. A feasible positive-consumption solution is assumed to exist.
hint: Use education and saving as the independent choices.
notes: Prompt continues onto user PDF page 22.

stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Write the first-order conditions for utility maximization.
solution: Differentiate the reduced objective. Its derivative with respect to $e$ is $[wh\prime(e)-(1+r)]/c_2$, giving the education condition. With respect to $s$ it is $-1/c_2+\beta/s=0$, equivalent to the Euler condition since $c_3=(1+r)s$. At $e=0$, replace equality by $wh\prime(0)\leq1+r$ when the derivative exists. Strict concavity of $h$ gives uniqueness of an interior education optimum; mere concavity allows multiple maximizers.
hint: Separate the return to education from the consumption Euler equation.

stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Derive the ratio $c_2/c_3$ in terms of the parameters.
solution: The saving FOC gives $s=\beta c_2$. Period-3 consumption is $(1+r)s=\beta(1+r)c_2$. Divide to obtain the stated ratio.
hint: Combine the Euler condition with old-age resources.

stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Explain how optimal investment in education depends on $\beta$.
answer: The education optimum is independent of $\beta$ under the stated unconstrained borrowing setup.
solution: Let net period-2 resources be $M(e)=wh(e)-(1+r)e$. Conditional optimal saving is $s=\beta M(e)/(1+\beta)$ and $c_2=M(e)/(1+\beta)$. Substitution into utility gives $(1+\beta)\log M(e)$ plus terms independent of $e$. Thus every $\beta>0$ gives the same education argmax, maximizing net resources. At an interior optimum $wh\prime(e)=1+r$, which has no $\beta$ term. Greater patience changes saving and the consumption split rather than education.
hint: Education is chosen to maximize lifetime resources.

stem: A street is $[0,1]$. Three agents live at $x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3$ and a hospital is located at $p\in[0,1]$. Find the square-optimal $p$ minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^3(x_i-p)^2$.
solution: The objective derivative is $6p-2\sum_i x_i$, which vanishes at the mean. Its second derivative is 6, so this is the unique minimum. The mean lies in $[0,1]$ and is feasible.
hint: Differentiate the sum of squared distances.

stem: A street is $[0,1]$. Three agents live at $x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3$ and a hospital is located at $p\in[0,1]$. An absolute-optimal $p$ minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^3|x_i-p|$. (i) Show an optimum lies in $[x_1,x_3]$. (ii) Derive an absolute-optimal location.
solution: If $p<x_1$, moving right reduces all three distances; if $p>x_3$, moving left does the same. Therefore neither can be optimal. For $p\in[x_1,x_3]$, the first and third distances sum to $x_3-x_1$, leaving objective $x_3-x_1+|p-x_2|$, uniquely minimized at $x_2$. The argument includes coincident locations.
hint: The extreme agents’ combined distance is constant between them.

stem: On street $[0,1]$, $n$ agents have ordered locations $x_1\leq\cdots\leq x_n$, where $n$ is odd. Derive $p$ minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-p|$.
solution: Pair the extreme locations: $(x_1,x_n),(x_2,x_{n-1}),\ldots$. Each pair contributes at least its separation, with equality whenever $p$ lies between that pair. All these intervals contain the median $m=x_{(n+1)/2}$. The unpaired median contributes $|p-m|$, which is zero only at $m$. Thus the median uniquely minimizes total distance.
hint: Pair locations symmetrically around the middle agent.

stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Derive $G(p)$ with clear explanation.
solution: The event is $x_1\leq p$ and $x_2\leq p$. Each has probability $p$; independence makes the joint probability $p^2$. Multiplication by $p$ gives $p^3$. If only uniform marginals are intended, the answer is instead $pH(p,p)$ for the joint CDF $H$, and is not determined: perfectly comoving uniforms give $p^2$, for example.
hint: Express the maximum event as the intersection of two events.
notes: Standard independent-draw interpretation used. Uniform marginals alone do not determine the joint distribution; independence is not explicitly stated in the source.

stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Plot $G(p)$.
answer: For independent draws, plot the increasing cubic $G(p)=p^3$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.
solution: Use points $(0,0),(1/4,1/64),(1/2,1/8),(3/4,27/64),(1,1)$. The curve starts with horizontal tangent, increases thereafter and becomes steeper toward 1. The graph presumes independent draws; uniform marginals without a joint distribution do not specify a unique graph.
hint: Use the cubic expression from part (a).
notes: Standard independent-draw interpretation used. Uniform marginals alone do not determine the joint distribution; independence is not explicitly stated in the source.

stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Is $G$ convex or concave in $p$? Explain.
answer: Under independent draws, strictly convex and not concave on $[0,1]$.
solution: For independent draws, $G(p)=p^3$ and $G\prime\prime(p)=6p\geq0$, positive for $p>0$. Thus it is strictly convex on the interval and fails concavity. The curvature conclusion relies on the joint-law assumption in part (a); uniform marginals alone do not fix $G$.
hint: Check the second derivative.
notes: Standard independent-draw interpretation used. Uniform marginals alone do not determine the joint distribution; independence is not explicitly stated in the source.

stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Find $\max_{p\in[0,1]}G(p)$.
solution: For every $p\in[0,1]$, $0\leq G(p)\leq p\leq1$. At $p=1$, both uniforms lie below 1 almost surely, so $G(1)=1$. For $p<1$, $G(p)\leq p<1$, so the maximizing point is unique. This conclusion needs no independence assumption.
hint: Bound the probability by one.

stem: Let $X\subset\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to X$. For continuous $f$ and $X=[0,1]$, use the intermediate value theorem to show there exists $x^*\in X$ with $f(x^*)=x^*$.
solution: Define $h(x)=f(x)-x$, continuous on $[0,1]$. Since $f$ maps the interval into itself, $h(0)=f(0)\geq0$ and $h(1)=f(1)-1\leq0$. If either is zero it is a fixed point; otherwise the intermediate value theorem supplies an interior zero.
hint: Apply the theorem to $f(x)-x$.

stem: Let $X\subset\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to X$. Determine whether fixed-point existence is guaranteed in each case, giving proof or counterexample: (i) $X=(0,1)$ and $f$ continuous; (ii) $X=[0,1]\cup[2,3]$ and $f$ continuous; (iii) $X=[0,1]$ but $f$ not continuous.
answer: No guarantee in any of the three cases.
solution: (i) $f(x)=(1+x)/2$ is a continuous self-map of $(0,1)$ whose only algebraic fixed point is 1, excluded from the domain. (ii) Set $f(x)=x+2$ on $[0,1]$ and $f(x)=x-2$ on $[2,3]$. This is continuous on the disconnected domain, maps it into itself and has no fixed point. (iii) Set $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x>0$. It maps $[0,1]$ into itself, is discontinuous and never equals $x$.
hint: Remove compactness, connectedness and continuity one at a time.

stem: Let $f_i:[0,1]\to[0,1]$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, be continuous. Prove there is $x^*\in[0,1]$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x^*)=mx^*$.
answer: Apply the fixed-point theorem to the average $F(x)=m^{-1}\sum_i f_i(x)$.
solution: The average $F$ is continuous and remains in $[0,1]$, because every summand lies there. The interval fixed-point argument in part (a) gives $F(x^*)=x^*$. Multiplying this equation by $m$ gives the required identity. Equivalently apply the intermediate value theorem directly to $\sum_i f_i(x)-mx$.
hint: An average of continuous interval self-maps is another such self-map.
